newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan April-September trade surplus plummets. [CORRECTED 17:20 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Japan April-September trade surplus plummets. [CORRECTED 17:20 GMT]

text.p: Japan's huge trade surplus plunged more than 40 percent in the first half of this fiscal year, a figure which should please Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto and U.S. President Bill Clinton as they head into elections.

The unadjusted customs-cleared trade surplus fell to 2.90 trillion yen ($25.8 billion) in the first half of the fiscal year which started in April, a drop of 41.6 percent, the Ministry of Finance (MOF) announced earlier on Friday.
It was the biggest drop since 1980 and came mainly from increases in imports of oil and office equipment, MOF said.
The trade surplus with the United States in the six-month period fell 24.2 percent from the previous year to 1.56 trillion yen ($13.9 billion).

The overall surplus for September alone fell 30.3 percent year-on-year to 779.52 billion (corrects from trillion) yen ($6.96 billion (corrects from trillion)), while the surplus with the United States fell 8.5 percent from a year earlier to 398.85 billion yen ($3.56 billion).

"They (the figures) are very good for everyone... The balance with the United States is coming down nicely... All the trade agreements between Japan and the United States are beginning to take effect," said Chris Pavlou, treasurer of global markets at Midland Bank in Tokyo.

Clinton would rather boast about the shrinking trade deficit with Japan as the result of past U.S. trade offensives ahead of the U.S. election on November 5 than mention brewing trade issues with Tokyo, economists said.
Japan's general election is on Sunday, and Hashimoto would be happy to see the falling surplus prevent another yen rally as Japan struggles to strengthen its recovery, they said.

Japan has traditionally been regarded as having an export-oriented economy. A strong yen would make Japanese products less competitive in overseas markets because it makes them more expensive in foreign currency terms.

"The trade surplus is still on a declining trend," a senior MOF official told reporters. He added that the volume of imports has shown continual growth for more than three years, at a pace that exceeds growth in the volume of exports.
Economists agree the surplus was continuing to shrink steadily, but say the pace of the drop was slowing.
"It (the surplus) could well stop falling by the beginning of 1997," said Chris Calderwood, chief economist at BZW Securities (Japan) Ltd.

Although a rise in global oil prices will put downward pressure on the trade surplus, firmer exports, especially of automobiles, would be a major factor in slowing the pace at which the surplus was shrinking, economists said.
"Generally, the yen is allowing them (exporters) to put their houses in order, cut prices and get back into markets more aggressively," Calderwood said.
The yen hit a record high of 79.75 to the dollar in April 1995 but since then it has slipped against the U.S. currency, trading at around 112 per dollar on Friday.
The dollar stayed steady in early Tokyo after the release of the trade data, as the figure was within expectations.

Other economists did not see any prospects for booming growth in exports as Japanese manufacturers, suffering from high costs at home and the strong yen, have already moved many of their production bases to other countries.
